title: Ecohydrological insight: Solar farms facilitate carbon sink enhancement in drylands
abstract:
Solar farms are critical to tackling climate change and achieving carbon neutrality. Besides producing renewable energy, a solar farm modifies microclimates and changes water distribution, consequently affecting local carbon sequestration capacity (CSC). Yet, how the CSC of an ecosystem responds to these changes after solar farm construction remains inadequately understood. Herein, the SOFAR model was adopted to reveal the effects of
large-scale solar farms (LSFs) on CSC in arid northern China, with a series of numeric experiments along a climate gradient (with precipitation ranging from 70 to 500 mm yr􀀀 1). The results show that relative to pristine vegetation background, CSC was non-linearly increased by averages of 3.49–6.68%, 4.43–10.25%, 5.07–9.71% and 5.6% each year after the installation of LSFs in hyper-arid climates (with aridity index or AI = 0.04–0.05), arid climates (AI = 0.14–0.16), semi-arid climates (AI = 0.21–0.3) and semi-humid climates (AI = 0.55), respectively. The increase in available water for plants growing under the drip lines of photovoltaic panels (PVs) in LSFs is
confirmed to be the overwhelming factor responsible for CSC enhancement. Although biases remain in the estimation of increased CSC in hyper- and semi-humid regions due to the high variability of climate (e.g., extreme drought events) and serious radiation reduction beneath PVs, it is certain that solar farms facilitate CSC without increasing external land use. These results will deepen our understanding of the feedback between solar
farms and ambient environments and be meaningful for vegetation management in solar farms, especially in the context of climate change and carbon neutrality aims.

## **1. Introduction**

A transition from carbon-intensive energy to affordable, accessible, and sustainable energy is essential to limit global warming to 2[◦] C above the pre-industrial level (Chu and Majumdar, 2012). Solar energy has been considered a viable climate and energy solution, and it usually tops the list of strategies the world can implement to stave off the worst effects of increasing temperatures, in any discussion regarding climate change (Creutzig et al., 2017; Dinçer, 2011; Zhao et al., 2011). As a result, the energy benefits of solar farms (i.e., directly reducing greenhouse gas emissions by substituting for carbon-intensive energy sources) have been widely recognized all over the world (Groesbeck and Pearce,

2018; Liu et al., 2022; Ye et al., 2021), whereas potential ecological impacts (i.e., additional carbon sink capacity from vegetation restoration or recolonization) throughout the long-term deployment of large-scale solar farms (LSFs) have rarely been investigated (Hernandez et al., 2019). LSFs have been deployed in various environments with varying and distinct plant-soil communities and climates, ranging from extremely arid to humid subtropical (Armstrong et al., 2014; Hamed and Alshare, 2022; Xia et al., 2022a). Through roof effects—i.e., concentrating rainfall into the drip lines, harvesting solar radiation and shading the ground (Jahanfar et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2022)—photovoltaic panels (PVs) can modify budgets of water, energy, and local or even regional environments (Hu et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2018). changes in microclimates and the deflection of rainfall could affect vegetation growth and microorganisms. For example, microorganisms are known to be beneficial to natural ecosystems (as they can facilitate biocrust restoration in LSFs (Yousefi et al., 2021Heredia-Velasquez  ́ ), et al., 2023), thereby affecting carbon sequestration (Armstrong et al., 2016; Green et al., 2019; Qin et al., 2021). Nevertheless, the impacts of LSFs on plants and carbon sequestration capacity (CSC) are poorly understood. And the results of studies that have been done have been mixed, with no consensus. In one study, for example, field observations indicated that the environment underneath a solar panel was a carbon source (Armstrong et al., 2016), but the opposite conclusion was also reported, at the same site, in a different study (Makaronidou, 2020).

Drylands are regions with an aridity index (AI, defined as the ratio of precipitation to potential evapotranspiration) lower than 0.65 (Li et al., 2021); they are the most abundant terrestrial biome on Earth (Schimel, 2010), and also of great interest for LSF application, due to their high solar potential (Tanner et al., 2020). Previous works have implied that land-intensive LSF deployment might bring additional carbon sequestration benefits to dryland ecosystems, through altered patterns of resources (i.e., rainfall and radiation), improved microclimates and increased plant productivity beneath the PVs (Armstrong et al., 2014). For example, Liu et al. (2019) reported that biomass beneath PVs was 30 times higher than that of the control site (i.e., an area outside the solar farm), and Adeh et al. (2019) also found 90% more dry biomass beneath PVs compared with the control site. However, such positive impacts are not universal, given the heterogeneities and complexities inherent in climatic drivers (e.g., rainfall and radiation). For instance, Liu (2020) and Armstrong et al. (2016) found 89% and 10% reductions in biomass in a solar farm, relative to the control, respectively. Evidently, the impacts of PVs on vegetation in LSFs can be climate- or location-dependent (Hamed and Alshare, 2022). In other words, the potential impacts of LSFs on local carbon sequestration may vary across climate gradients, more likely depending on _where_ they are deployed (rather than _how many_ are deployed), but quantification data (e.g., biomass and ecosystem respiration) across climate gradients, and information about related approaches (e.g., non-destructive measuring methods of biomass, and specific models for solar farms) remain lacking (Armstrong et al., 2014).

Field experiments and model simulations are the two major approaches to assessing the environmental impacts of LSFs. The PV-altered ecohydrological processes and ecosystem services within LSFs have been reported based on both in-situ field experiments and regional-scale modelling efforts. For example, recent field studies have reported changes in biomass (Liu, 2020; Liu et al., 2019), energy balance (Jiang et al., 2021) and carbon exchange (Armstrong et al., 2016; Makaronidou, 2020), and have discussed the mechanism by which PVs affect ecohydrological processes (Armstrong et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2022). Through regional modelling efforts, Hu et al. (2016) found that super LSFs changed regional temperature and precipitation; Yang et al. (2018) reported local temperature increase and twofold precipitation increase in the Sahara, caused by LSFs, because the PVs reduced surface albedo and thus triggered a positive albedo-precipitation-vegetation feedback; and Lu et al. (2021) even indicated that a hypothetical LSF could increase vegetation cover through enhanced atmosphere–land–vegetation feedbacks. Compared with the abundance of studies at panel and regional scales, mesoscale (e.g., whole-farm scale) studies are less numerous but more desirable for practical application. For one thing, a photovoltaic array is not a complete landscape unit. In-situ field observations under PVs are hampered in their ability to be upscaled to represent the cumulative effect of an entire solar farm over its life-span, due to the inherent heterogeneity of soil and topography, and the slowly changing field CSC dynamics (Baartman et al., 2018; Cabal et al., 2021). Furthermore, the possible impacts reported at regional scales have yet to be verified by observations or mesoscale evidence (Chang et al., 2020), and the mapping results of LSFs also have shown that no intense, high-capacity concentrated scheme (e.g., _>_ 1 GW) research model at the

regional scale actually exists (Xia et al., 2022a). As a result, both field observations and regional modelling results are difficult to apply in real-life situations, and the derived conclusions about the impacts of LSFs on ecosystems may be biased due to the lack of mesoscale evidence.

Therefore, a mesoscale (i.e., whole-farm) evaluation scheme and a more elaborate model that can capture microclimate changes and rainfall redistribution incurred by PVs are necessary, to understand how local modifications incurred by LSFs control the long-term dynamics of the water and carbon footprints of local ecosystems. A water-carbon coupled model (the Solar-Farm model, SOFAR) we recently developed was applied in this study, to determine the impacts of LSFs on vegetation dynamics and the CSC across the climate gradient (Liu et al., 2023). In the model, locally refined grids were adopted to capture the changes in microclimates beneath PVs—changes that remain unresolved from previous studies. Given that LSFs have been built under various climate conditions and in various land use types (Kruitwagen et al., 2021), and considering the reported findings of Adeh et al. (2018) (‘more water and reduced irradiance facilitate productivity increase in arid lands, but a serious reduction of radiation ( _>_ 50%) may inhibit plant growth in semi-humid lands’), we hypothesize that there is a non-linear and non-monotonic tendency of the net CSC of an LSF when the ecosystem changes from arid to semi-humid lands. Eight idealized numerical simulation scenarios were performed using the SOFAR model at both the panel and farm levels. Through this effort, we aimed to: (1) reveal what impacts an LSFs has on CSC, (2) understand how biotic and abiotic factors are coordinated in an LSF, to affect vegetation dynamics and CSC, and (3) verify the nonlinear and non-monotonic hypotheses and determine the best placement for an LSF, to enhance the CSC most significantly following the installation of an LSF. This study provides a feasible method for simulating the water-carbon dynamics in LSFs at mesoscales, and thus is meaningful for the vegetation management and the improvement of the ecological functions of LSFs.

## **2. Material and methods**

## _2.1. Study area and field observations_

Northern China is a massive region with tremendous variations in climate and land use. The eight selected scenarios in this study correspond to the drylands in northern China, ranging from hyper-arid regions to semi-humid regions (Fig. 1a). These regions have abundant solar energy resources and large available lands, making them ideal for LSF development. An experimental site (hereafter, the Hongsibu site) was selected within a solar farm (with a capacity of 200 MW) at the Hongsibu district of Wuzhong City in Ningxia Autonomous Region of arid northern China (37[◦] 25[′] 30.17[′′] N, 106[◦] 3[′] 27.58[′′] E) (Fig. 1b). At the Hongsibu site, PVs are arranged in east–west–oriented rows and inclined southward at a tilt angle of 37.2[◦] ; the row spacing of the PVs is about 8.5 m, and the length and width of the individual photovoltaic panels are 2 m and 1 m, respectively. Annual precipitation is approximately 186 mm based on the last 38 years (1980–2017 inclusive) of available meteorological records at the Wuzhong weather station, which is about 30 km away from the solar farm. The soil consists mainly of loess soil. The predominant vegetation outside the solar farm is perennial shrubs ( _Reaumuria soongarica_ ). However, within the solar farm, these shrubs were removed during the construction period and the area was then colonized by annual ( _sweet wormwood_ ) and perennial ( _Stipa capillata_ ) grasses, which are artificially mowed annually to avoid fire hazard and the loss of PV efficiency that could be caused by the plants shading the PVs.

The area below the PVs was divided into five sections—Front, Shade, Middle, Back and Gap (Fig. 1b)—according to different water and light conditions. The volumetric moisture content (VWC) was measured at each of these parts, at multiple layers (10, 20, 40, and 60 cm) using TDR probes (ECH2O, Decagon, Inc), and data (from April 27, 2021 to 19/11/ 2021) were collected at 10-min scan intervals. The aboveground biomass of the Control was estimated from UAV images using a volumetric method, which is based on measured species volume units developed from total standing biomass measurements (Muldavin et al., 2008).

## _2.2. SOFAR model_

As shown in Fig. 1d, the SOFAR model was adopted to quantify the ecological processes and physical processes at a daily time step (Liu et al., 2023), including rainfall interception (Elamri et al., 2018) and radiation harvesting of the PVs (Diez et al., 2021; Passias and Kallb ̈ ack,  ̈ 1984), soil moisture dynamics, and vegetation evolution. These processes were described as the following differential equations, and more details of the model can be found in the Supplementary Material. The model mainly focuses on the potential carbon input into the ecosystem through photosynthesis of the vegetation (hereafter, carbon sequestration), and is driven by daily meteorological variables including precipitation, maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and sunshine duration. ## _2.3. Climate scenarios selection_

Terrestrial carbon dynamic intertwines with vegetation dynamics, which are dominated by energy and water availability (Green et al., 2019 ). However, there are significant discrepancies between different climate regions in terms of energy and water. In this study, eight climate scenarios considering vegetation differences and climatic gradients (without anthropogenic intervention) with AI ranging from 0.05 to 0.55 (Fig. 1a), including hyper-arid, arid, semi-arid, and semi-humid climates, were performed by the SOFAR model (Table 1). ## **3. Results**

## _3.1. Parameterization and model validation_

## _2.4. Analysis method_

For each climate scenario, there were two simulation experiments, including a scenario with PVs and a scenario without PVs (which was considered to be the benchmark for CSC). For the scenario with PVs, the vegetation consisted of grass and shrubs; however, for the scenario without PVs, the vegetation was all shrubs. Accordingly, the effects of solar farms on CSC, i.e., net CSC (g DM yr[−][1] ), was calculated as the net primary productivity ( _NPP_ ) of the scenario with PVs ( _NPPPVs)_ minus the _NPP_ of the scenario without PVs ( _NPP No PVs_ ), wherein NPP was calculated as the difference of gross primary productivity ( _GPP_ , i.e., photosynthetic carbohydrates) and respiration ( _Res_ , the sum of _Rat_ and _Rrt_ ).

Water use efficiency (WUE) is used to assess the impact of PVs on vegetation productivity per unit of water used. At the ecosystem level, WUE is calculated as the ratio of GPP to evapotranspiration (ET) (Knauer et al., 2017).

The statistical index, Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency coefficient (NSE), was used for assessing the accuracy of the SOFAR model.

The field observations of VWC at the Hongsibu site (from April 27, 2021 to 06/09/2021) were used to validate the simulation results of the SOFAR model. Field aboveground biomass was collected on 17/07/ 2021 (the middle of the growing season) and 17/09/2022 (the end of the growing season), and determined using destructive plant sampling. The data were then used as a validation of the predicted highest biomass through the growing season. Soil porosity ( _n_ ) and field capacity ( _Sfc_ ) were measured as 0.55 and 0.4, respectively, at the laboratory. The corresponding values of other parameters are given in Table S1; these were calibrated using the genetic algorithm method with the Nash– Sutcliffe efficiency coefficient (NSE) as the fitness function. The simulation results of soil moisture were tested against field observations, capturing the magnitudes of soil moisture responses to rainfall pulses and persistent evapotranspiration loss (NSE = 0.52–0.85) (Fig. 2).

## _3.3. Enhanced transpiration below PVs_

Our results showed that both transpiration and evaporation were increased beneath the PVs, compared with the scenarios without the installation of PVs. As shown in Fig. 4a–h, soil evaporation contributes most of the soil water loss (i.e., _T_ / _ET <_ 0.5) in Scenarios S1 to S4, and transpiration loss overwhelms soil evaporation when the climatic becomes wetter. Overall, the increase in transpiration is higher than that of soil evaporation, beneath the PVs. Specifically, the ratio of transpiration to evapotranspiration increased approximately two times underneath the PVs in hyper-arid regions and arid regions. In semi-arid regions and semi-humid regions, however, these increases were not obvious, with increases of 8–36% (Fig. 4a–h). Similar to the increase in _ET_ , the increase in GPP also was confirmed by our projected results (Fig. S2). The most obvious increase in GPP was found in Scenario S1 (hyper-arid region). However, the average increase in GPP (102%) was lower than that of ET (242%) (Fig. S2), compared with the scenarios without the installation of LSFs. Consequently, inconsistent with investing more water into transpiration, water use efficiency ( _WUE_ ) showed little change after PV installation, and there was no universal trend in the changes in _WUE_ . _WUE_ decreased by 8.9% and 6.2% in hyper-arid and

## _3.4. CSC of the whole farm_

Our results confirmed that the CSC of the whole farm increased by up to 3.48–10.25% in comparison with a pristine vegetation background in a dryland ecosystem (with 76–506 mm yr[−][1] ), after the installation of the LSF. Projected net CSC at the whole solar farm presents a nonlinear and non-monotonic tendency (Fig. 5a), with the average CSC varying from 3.29 × 10[4 ] kg DM yr[−][1 ] to 12.82 × 10[5 ] kg DM yr[−][1 ] along the climate gradient, from 76 mm yr[−][1 ] to 506 mm yr[−][1 ] of precipitation. The highest increase of CSC (10.25%) was found in Scenario S5. Furthermore, predicted results showed that the carbon sequestration enhancement is not uniform across the whole solar farm. The most conspicuous carbon sink enhancement occurred in the areas within the solar farms with the highest installation densities of PVs (Fig. 6e), as well as in the central areas of the photovoltaic arrays (Fig. 5b–i).

## **4. Discussion**

## _4.1. Do solar farms facilitate carbon sequestration in dryland ecosystems?_

Globally, soil loses 1.6 ± 0.8 Pg C each year due to land use changes (Smith, 2008). Installation of an LSF often incurs intensive land use

change: arable land, forest, and scrubland have been used to install LSFs (Kruitwagen et al., 2021), accompanied by construction activities including vegetation clearing and grubbing, topsoil stripping, land grading and leveling, and soil compaction (Fig. 6c) (Choi et al., 2020). As a result, there is a concern that unforeseen carbon loss could occur due to this land use change and ecological state transition (e.g., from shrublands to grasslands) (Moscatelli et al., 2022).

Previous field observations and modelling results have shown that the impacts of LSFs are more likely to be beneficial than detrimental for carbon sequestration (Yang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2021). Our results also support this conclusion and indicate that LSFs facilitate carbon sequestration in dryland ecosystems, and this positive impact is the most significant for arid and semi-arid regions (Fig. 5a). Meanwhile, a declining trend in net CSC was found from the predicted results when the climate becomes drier or wetter relative to the semi-arid regions. This nonlinear and non-monotonic tendency of the net CSC of LSFs detected across the climate gradient proved our hypothesis, which is also supported by sporadic observation results (Adeh et al., 2018; Armstrong et al., 2016; Du and Sun, 2017; Liu, 2020; Liu et al., 2019; Moscatelli et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021) (Fig. 6a). For example, Liu et al. (2019) found that the biomass in a solar farm was approximately 25 times higher than that of a control site in a sandy desert ecosystem (about 200 mm precipitation per year), as well as a 6.75-fold increase in vegetation coverage. However, the temporal dynamics of the CSC of LSFs were ignored in most previous research, and we argue that the short-term and restricted spatial range considered in previous field results may weaken the existing conclusions about the impacts of LSFs on CSC. For example, a contradictory conclusion about carbon exchange beneath PVs was reported at a solar farm built in a temperate UK grassland, and this discrepancy was attributed to differences in annual climate conditions and the selection of sampling days (Armstrong et al., 2016; Makaronidou, 2020). Accordingly, whether the impact of LSFs on CSC is always positive at a given site during long-term deployment, could be a question to debate. Our further results consolidate considerable inter-annual variabilities in the estimated net CSC of LSFs (Fig. S1). Thus, we believe that the impacts of LSFs on CSC are not consistent over time. Such a judgment is also supported by a few other reported findings (Makaronidou, 2020).

The spatial and temporal variations involved in the estimated potentials of CSC increase by LSFs may be mainly attributed to two aspects: (1) Inversion of water limitation and light limitation. Serious water scarcity in arid lands (AI _<_ 0.2) may not provide enough support for the

vegetation to complete its life cycle, and the higher respiration and senescence rates of grasses in LSFs usually lead to a more sensitive dependence of carbon exchange on local soil moisture variation relative to the more drought-tolerant shrubs in surrounding areas (Petrie et al., 2015). However, in semi-humid areas where water is not such a limitation, light competition underneath PVs could become the dominant factor driving plant productivity in LSFs (Adeh et al., 2018). As a result, compared with arid regions, the difference in CSC, between grasses and shrubs, is reduced in semi-humid regions, because of increase in water availability and more intense radiation reduction, respectively. For example, recently published literatures show that photosynthetically active radiation, rather than soil moisture content, dominates vegetation growth under PVs in semi-arid regions (Li et al., 2023; Sturchio et al., 2022), provided that other resources are accessible at copious levels (Mamun et al., 2023), whereas soil moisture content causes a striped pattern of vegetation in arid regions (Liu et al., 2019). However, it cannot be overemphasized that vegetation and soil heterogeneities impact the observed results of an LSF’s effects on plant productivity. (2) Interannual variability of climatic drivers. Given that annual rainfall variability can be expected to inevitably propagate into the soil moisture system, rapid swings in productivity and even shifts in the state of carbon sinks and carbon sources are very likely to occur between deficient and abundant rainfall periods (Hutley et al., 2022). Accordingly, for the warming and wetting drylands in arid northern China, inferred from data from the last 38 years (1980–2017 inclusive) of observation records at the weather station (Fig. 6b), it is expected that the revealed positive effects of LSFs on plant productivity will be intensified, and thus potentially incur broader and even more far-reaching implications on regional ecosystem services in the future (Xia et al., 2022b).

## _4.2. How does a solar farm affect local carbon sequestration?_

In response to the installation of LSFs, transitions in the vegetation

community and changes in plant productivity occur in LSFs (Xia et al., 2022b). Notable progress has been made in understanding how large-scale farms (LSFs) affect vegetation growth, and this effect could be attributed to changes in microclimates and the deflection of rainfall caused by photovoltaic panels (PVs) (Uldrijan et al., 2022). However, there is lack of the comprehensive understanding of mechanisms regarding how LSFs affect vegetation growth and productivity, due to the short observation times and the restricted geographic ranges considered in most field studies. Adeh et al. (2018), for example, attributed the positive net CSC of LSFs to enhanced WUE; however, this conclusion is not fully supported by our results (Fig. 4i). According to the definition of WUE (Eq. (6)), the decline of WUE in this study was attributed to a higher increase of ET (average of 242%) compared to that of GPP (average of 102%), relative to the scenario without the installation of PVs (Fig. S2). Accordingly, it may be problematic to attribute the increase of biomass in LSFs to the change of WUE. Instead, biomass increase in LSFs is more likely due to enhanced soil water content and mitigated radiation stress, based on our results. The widely accepted view among scientists is that PVs affect local carbon sequestration by changing the spatial distribution of rainfall and modifying

microclimates (Adeh et al., 2018; Armstrong et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2019), i.e., (1) PVs harvest incident radiation and shade the ground, which leads to serious reduction of photosynthetically active radiation under the PVs. For example, it has been reported that photosynthetically active radiation under PVs is 67%–92% lower than that in the area outside the LSFs (Armstrong et al., 2016; Li et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2019; Noor and Reeza, 2022); and (2) imperious PVs intercept rainfall and concentrate it onto the downslope edge as a downpour, which could increase the available water under the downslope edge of PVs by a factor of five (Wu et al., 2022). Furthermore, PVs modify other microclimate factors (e.g., wind speed, temperature, humidity), further regulating vegetation growth and reshaping vegetation compositions (Uldrijan et al., 2021, 2022).

Based on our results, we argue that the results of the conflict between more available water and less radiation determine the impacts of these solar farms on plants. Drylands are subjected to infrequent rainfall and excess irradiance, and thus plants in these ecosystems are potentially exposed to both water stress and photoinhibition (Müller-Xing et al., 2014). Impervious PVs in LSFs offer more moderate microclimates relative to natural conditions due to the roof effects. Although the cover rate of PVs in a solar farm as a whole might be low (28–34%), the amount of available water for plants along the drip lines (below the downslope edge of the PVs) when precipitation occurs, can reach about five times higher than natural rainfall (Wu et al., 2022) and irradiance could be reduced by 67–90% (Armstrong et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019; Tanner et al., 2020). The significantly lowered water and light stresses are enough to trigger significant ecological feedbacks and unintended ecological consequences (Wu et al., 2022). For example, in relatively dry environments, better soil water status throughout the growing season might support more vigorous vegetative growth (Adeh et al., 2018), as evidenced by the higher biomass of Front and Middle compared with other areas beneath PVs (Fig. 3a) and to the increased ratio of transpiration to evaporation below PVs (Fig. 4a–h). PVs could thus facilitate carbon sink enhancement in these areas. In contrast, if LSFs are built in semi-humid environments (AI = 0.3–0.55) with abundant rainfall but moderate irradiance, the net primary productivity below PVs is expected to decrease, due to energy limitation (compared with water availability) caused by serious radiation reduction (Armstrong et al., 2016).

In view of the diverse impacts of LSFs on vegetation, which have been observed globally, we argue that climate and vegetation compositions determine the background value of CSC of a natural ecosystem, and LSFs further divert the natural ecosystem from its normal evolutionary track and change CSC, but these effects depend on the climate and vegetation background (Armstrong et al., 2014). Thus, we propose a conceptual model as three hierarchies: climate, vegetation, and PV disturbance. Climate acts as a filter, primarily determining the initial pools of primeval vegetation and the potential carbon sequestration of terrestrial ecosystems. Physiological discrepancies in plants further cause the CSCs of terrestrial ecosystems to differ. For example, the more drought-tolerant characteristics of shrubs in arid conditions allow resources to access and capture more CO2 than grass, under natural con-

ditions (Petrie et al., 2015). However, the CSC of shrubs is lower than that of grasses when both grow to full size, because the annual capacity of shrubs to fix carbon reaches a constant or near-saturation level (i.e., potential carbon sequestration of shrubs) (He et al., 2017). Compared with shrubs, the annual capacity of grasses can increase more quickly, because grasses grow rapidly from the root each season, or from seed in response to rainfall, and thus produce more biomass (Fig. 6d). Similar productivity differences between grass and trees have been reported in savanna ecosystems (Hutley et al., 2022). Finally, the installation of LSFs acts as a disturbance that alters the existing vegetation communities and microclimates, ultimately increasing the spatial heterogeneity of CSC, and the strength of this perturbation is related to the efficiency and geometrical dimension of the PVs. Therefore, we emphasize here again that the impacts of LSFs on CSC are climate- and location-dependent; however, the universal mechanisms of how PVs

affect local CSC are explained by the roof effects (Jahanfar et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2022).

## _4.3. Uncertainty analysis and future perspectives_

The SOFAR model presented in this study simulates the water and carbon fluxes in LSFs and is capable of adequately capturing the dynamics of soil moisture, vegetation evolution, and productivity. However, the failure to consider the spatial heterogeneities of soil parameters and landform characteristics in this study could incur uncertainties in the predicted results (Bouaziz et al., 2022), given that landform controls the runoff and infiltration processes and soil plays an essential role in the resource availability of plants (Shanjia Li et al., 2018a,b). To evaluate the impacts of soil parameters and landforms on the predicted results, three additional numerical experiments were conducted. The uniform soil parameters ( _Ks, Sfc,_ and _Sh_ ) were replaced with heterogeneous parameters, and the hill landform was replaced with a flat landform. Predicted net CSC was slightly increased, by 3.91%, when homogeneous soil parameters were replaced by heterogeneous soil parameters in semi-arid Scenario S5 (Fig. 7a). However, net CSC decreased 168.45% and 158.21%, when the hill landform was replaced with a flat landform, in semi-humid scenarios S7 and S8 respectively (Fig. 7b and c). These results indicated that landform has a greater influence on predicted results than do soil parameters. However, the spatial patterns of CSC that were affected by LSFs in our study are still consistent with other reported results (Adeh et al., 2018; Armstrong et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2021). Correspondingly, although these simplifications may be significant for specific cases, they have a limited impact on our main findings and conclusions, especially when considering the objectives of this study: to reveal the climate pattern impact of LSFs on net CSC, across the climate gradient.

Besides parameter uncertainties, additional uncertainties may arise from the parameterization schemes in the model and the simplified plant types. For example, there was a 62% increase in biomass for the _L. chinensis_ community in the solar farm as compared to the control site. However, a 5–24% decline was found when there were different plant communities between the solar farm ( _stipa capillata_ , _dogstail_ ) and the control site ( _Artemisia frigida_ , _stipa capillata_ ) (Du and Sun, 2017). Although these uncertainties may incur deviations in the values of CSC, their impact on our main conclusion about the nonlinear and non-monotonic tendency for the net CSC of LSFs reported in this study is limited because the SOFAR model considered major physiological processes, unlike other models (Istanbulluoglu et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2013), and field results from other vegetation communities (Fig. 6a) have also supported our findings. Furthermore, discrepant vegetation communities and nutrient limitations on plant growth should be coupled into the model in future studies based on additional field observations, because the omission of nitrogen limitation in carbon sequestration evaluation models has been criticized for being unjustified from an ecological point of view and even for overrating carbon sequestration in the soil-plant continuum (Goll et al., 2012).

Our results show that LSFs can facilitate CSC under a scenario without anthropogenic management, so that CSC values attributable to LSFs, higher than those reported in this study, can be expected if reasonable vegetation management schemes are adopted. Given the globally unprecedented expansion of LSFs and the positive results predicted by this study, vegetation management schemes and carbon exchange of LSFs will be more and more likely to be a concern in further research about LSFs (Armstrong et al., 2014). Vegetation recolonization or regeneration in LSFs can increase carbon sequestration (Lal, 2018), by supporting biodiversity and protecting against water and wind erosion (Quijano-Baron et al., 2022). However, unmanaged vegetation might Vaverkova  ́ incur fire hazards and could shade the photovoltaic panels ( et al., 2022). Consequently, reasonable vegetation management schemes need further investigation to achieve a win-win situation for ecological and energy benefits. This study mainly focused on the impact

of LSFs on plant productivity; however, soil, as the biggest carbon pool, contains three times more organic carbon than global vegetation and the atmosphere combined (Bossio et al., 2020; Caruso et al., 2018; Lehmann and Kleber, 2015). Accordingly, more robust models warrant further research to reveal the impact of LSFs on not only vegetation productivity but also soil organic carbon, as well as ecosystem respiration, which was not included in this study but which has a considerable impact on carbon dynamics in ecosystems (Petrie et al., 2015). Finally, more _in-situ_ field observations (e.g., biomass, ecosystem carbon exchange, and long-term vegetation revegetation or restoration experiments) across various landscapes and climates are needed, in order to understand the impacts of building LSFs under various conditions.

## **5. Conclusions**

This study, based on a water-carbon coupled model (SOFAR model) and _in-situ_ field observations, provides the first mesoscale results of impacts of LSFs on CSC, and reveals that: (1) LSFs may facilitate carbon sequestration in dryland ecosystems; (2) the pattern of the impacts of LSFs on CSC along the climate gradient is nonlinear; (3) the positive impact of LSFs on CSC is most significant for arid and semi-arid regions; and (4) plant type transition (e.g., from shrublands to grasslands) and the roof effects of PVs are responsible for how LSFs can affect local CSC. Our findings can guide site selection for LSFs and vegetation management inside LSFs. Globally, LSFs have been deployed in various landscapes with varying and distinct plant-soil communities and climates. Thus, the installation of LSFs might incur conflicts between energy generation and ecosystem functions (e.g., carbon sequestration). Our results show that the detrimental effects of LSFs on ecosystems can be mitigated or even eliminated through vegetation restoration and revegetation. However, more robust models and field observations (e.g., biomass, ecosystem carbon exchange, and long-term vegetation, revegetation, or restoration experiments) warrant further research.
